title: Mean-payoff games in polynomial time
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in the total input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E), a\) partition \(V=V_{\mathrm{Max}}\sqcup V_{\mathrm{Min}}\), integer edge weights \(w:E\to Z\), and a start vertex s, determine whether Max has a strategy \(\sigma\) such that every strategy \(\tau\) of Min produces a play \(s=v_{0},v_{1},\ldots\) satisfying \(\liminf _{T\to \infty}(1/T) \sum _{t=0}^{T- 1} w(v_{t},v_{t+1})\ge 0\).
definitions: The graph, its ownership partition, its start vertex and all weights are represented explicitly; weights use signed binary. Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge, so plays are infinite. The owner of the current vertex chooses the next edge with full knowledge of the finite history. Strategies are arbitrary deterministic functions of this history. There are no chance vertices, simultaneous moves, hidden observations or multiple payoff coordinates. Max seeks a nonnegative lower limit of average accumulated weight; equality zero is winning. No bound is imposed on intermediate losses or on the size \(\mathrm{W}=\max (1,\max _{e} |w(e)|)\). The running-time requirement concerns ordinary bit operations, so a polynomial dependence on W is not sufficient. Zero threshold loses no generality: a binary rational threshold \(a/b\) with \(b>0\) can be absorbed by replacing \(w(e)\) with \(b w(e)- a\), with polynomial growth of the encoding.
answer_criterion: Prove that this exact winner-decision language is in P, or prove that it is outside P. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a smoothed or average-case guarantee, or a lower bound for one strategy-improvement rule does not settle the unrestricted worst-case question. Strongly polynomial time would suffice but is a stronger requirement than this card asks for.
why: A foundational complexity question for long-run adversarial optimization. It connects finite graph games, quantitative verification, resource reasoning and tropical algebra, with short optimal strategies but no known polynomial-time method to find the winner on arbitrary binary-weighted inputs.

importance.reason: A canonical NP∩coNP problem central to quantitative synthesis and long-run control; resolving the binary-weight complexity gap would have consequences across several equivalent algebraic and game formulations.

progress.text: Zwick and Paterson give pseudopolynomial algorithms, establish the complexity framework, and reduce mean-payoff games to simple stochastic games.
Brim, Chaloupka, Doyen, Gentilini and Raskin obtain O(nmW) arithmetic-operation bounds for threshold decision and winning-strategy synthesis via energy games.
Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann derive tight bounds for value iteration using universal graphs, a restricted algorithmic framework.

Loff and Skomra publish smoothed polynomial guarantees for games on ergodic graphs with independently perturbed rewards. The published theorem includes the ergodicity restriction omitted from the earlier arXiv abstract.
Maat’s preprint gives direct connections between strategy improvement and simplex variants under nondegeneracy assumptions, without a general polynomial iteration bound.
Adenwalla and coauthors give connections to graph-class chromatic boundedness and explicitly retain the general polynomial-time question in §3.7.2.

status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The July 2026 primary source explicitly states that polynomial-time solution with binary weights remains open. The card fixes a single deterministic mean-payoff objective with a nonnegative liminf threshold. Pseudopolynomial, ergodic smoothed-analysis and framework-specific results do not resolve arbitrary worst-case inputs.

context_blocks.text: Mean payoff measures sustainable long-run performance. Edge weights can represent net resource gains, rewards or the negative of costs; an adversary controls some of the transitions. A finite initial loss disappears from the limiting average, while a repeatedly traversed cycle continues to matter. For example, eventually repeating weights −5 and +7 has mean payoff one, regardless of any fixed initial prefix. This distinguishes the objective from requiring the accumulated sum to remain nonnegative at every step.

Optimal positional strategies exist for both players, so a player can make the same choice whenever a vertex is revisited. With both choices fixed, the resulting path eventually repeats a cycle, and its value is the cycle’s average weight. This yields compact certificates and \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) membership. It does not make the search easy: the number of positional strategy combinations can be exponential. Zwick and Paterson gave the classical complexity analysis and a polynomial reduction to simple stochastic games.

The size of a weight and the size of its representation differ sharply. A weight \(2^{b}\) takes only \(b+1\) binary digits. An algorithm using O(nmW) arithmetic operations, where n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges, can therefore take exponential time in the input length. Brim and coauthors obtain such a pseudopolynomial bound for the threshold problem through energy-game progress measures. The result is powerful for small weights, but it leaves the dependence needed for this question unresolved.

Universal graphs provide a way to organize and compare value-iteration algorithms. Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann establish tight bounds within that framework, including improved dependence on the largest weight for a fixed number of vertices. Such a matching lower bound identifies a limitation of the framework being analyzed; it does not rule out an unrelated polynomial-time algorithm for mean-payoff games.

Smoothed analysis gives a different kind of progress. Loff and Skomra’s ICALP 2024 theorem obtains polynomial running time with high probability after sufficiently random independent perturbations of rewards, on ergodic game graphs. Here ergodicity is stronger than ordinary strong connectivity: for every reward assignment, the game value is independent of the start vertex. The theorem helps explain efficiency on perturbed inputs while retaining both a graph restriction and distributional assumptions. It does not decide the present worst-case complexity question.

There are also increasingly direct links to linear optimization. Maat’s September 2025 preprint identifies many strategy-improvement variants with instances of the simplex algorithm under nondegeneracy assumptions. This gives a structural bridge between algorithms and their lower-bound constructions. A correspondence between local improvement methods, however, is not a proof that their number of iterations is polynomial.

A July 2026 preprint by Adenwalla and coauthors connects tropical inequality systems and mean-payoff games with deciding chromatic boundedness for certain classes of graphs defined by equality patterns. Its reverse encoding uses a specified succinct representation. This creates another setting in which a solver would be useful. The paper explicitly leaves polynomial-time mean-payoff solving open, and its graph-class reduction should not be mistaken for a polynomial algorithm for games.

sentences: In a mean-payoff game, two players move a token through a finite weighted directed graph.
The maximizing player wants the limiting lower average weight to be nonnegative against every opposing strategy.
The project asks whether this threshold question has a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the full binary input length.
Algorithms polynomial in the numerical magnitude of weights do not suffice because a large weight can have a short encoding.
An efficient solution would settle a central exact optimization problem for systems with long-run rewards and adversarial control.
